notes:
Task and constraints: Find the longest uppercase-letter substring that can be made uniform using at most k replacements.
Idea: Maintain a sliding window and the highest frequency seen for any character in that window.
Technique and why it applies: A window is feasible when its length minus the dominant character count is at most k. When it exceeds that bound, the left edge advances once; max_count is intentionally kept as a historical maximum rather than recomputed.
Invariant: The current window is adjusted by at most one position per right-step, and max_length records the largest window length observed.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero. The method assumes uppercase English characters as specified.
Complexity: Each character enters and leaves the window at most once, giving O(n) time and O(u) space for the frequency dictionary, where u is at most 26.

Task and constraints: Maximize the length of a substring that can be converted to one repeated character using at most k changes.
Idea: Expand a sliding window and track its maximum character frequency, shrinking when the current length requires too many replacements.
Technique and why it applies: result is the current best window length. If result - max_count reaches k before adding another valid length, the left-side character is removed; otherwise the best length grows.
Invariant: The algorithm tracks a nondecreasing best length and adjusts counts as the right pointer advances.
Edge cases: Empty s returns zero. max_count is not reduced when the left edge moves, a standard optimization for this length-only result rather than an exact frequency for every window.
Complexity: One pass with constant expected dictionary operations gives O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space for the fixed uppercase alphabet.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of single-character mutations needed to change start into end using only genes in bank.
Idea: Run breadth-first search over bank strings, connecting genes that differ in exactly one position.
Technique and why it applies: The queue stores the current frontier. For each dequeued gene, the code compares it with every unused bank gene and enqueues those with exactly one differing character; each queue layer represents one more mutation.
Invariant: used prevents a bank entry from being enqueued more than once, and dist counts BFS layers.
Edge cases: The code references deque but does not import it, so it fails unless deque is supplied externally. If end is absent from bank, it cannot be reached and the method returns -1.
Complexity: Comparing every pair of bank strings costs O(B²·8), effectively O(B²) for fixed length eight, with O(B) queue/visited storage. The unused last index does not change the search.

Task and constraints: Return the shortest mutation sequence length from start to end, using only valid bank genes and one-character changes.
Idea: Use BFS from start, generating all one-character mutations and enqueueing those present in the bank that have not been visited.
Technique and why it applies: BFS explores paths in increasing mutation count, so the first time end is dequeued its level is minimal. lookup records bank membership and visitation status.
Invariant: Every queued pair contains a gene reachable at the recorded number of mutations, and visited genes are not queued again.
Edge cases: If start equals end, the initial queue returns zero. An end gene not in bank is never generated and results in -1.
Complexity: Each visited gene generates 8×4 candidate strings, each of length eight, giving O(B) effective time for fixed gene length and alphabet, with O(B) storage for lookup and queue.

Task and constraints: Count contiguous non-space segments in a string.
Idea: Split the string on whitespace and count the resulting nonempty tokens.
Technique and why it applies: Python's split without an explicit separator treats runs of whitespace as separators and omits empty pieces, so its list length equals the number of segments.
Invariant: Every token in the split result corresponds to one non-space segment from the original string.
Edge cases: Empty strings and strings containing only spaces return zero. This behavior also treats tabs and other whitespace as separators, not just the literal space character.
Complexity: Splitting scans the string in O(n) time and creates tokens requiring O(n) additional space in the worst case.

Task and constraints: Count the non-space segments separated by spaces in s.
Idea: Count a segment whenever a space follows a non-space character, and account separately for a final non-space character.
Technique and why it applies: Every segment boundary has a transition from non-space to space; the initial result is one only if the string is nonempty and does not end in a space.
Invariant: result counts all completed segments seen at transitions plus a possible final segment.
Edge cases: Empty strings return zero through int(len(s) and ...). The code treats only the literal space character as a separator, unlike split(), which recognizes all whitespace.
Complexity: One scan gives O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, consistent with the author labels.

Task and constraints: Remove the fewest intervals so the remaining intervals do not overlap.
Idea: Sort intervals by start and keep the smallest possible end among overlapping intervals.
Technique and why it applies: If a new interval starts after the current retained end, it can be kept and prevEnd advances. On overlap, count one removal and retain whichever interval ends earlier, leaving more room for later intervals.
Invariant: prevEnd is the end of the retained interval with the earliest end among the overlapping choices processed so far.
Edge cases: The code assumes intervals is nonempty because it accesses intervals[0]. Equal endpoints are treated as non-overlapping via start >= prevEnd.
Complexity: Sorting takes O(n log n), and the scan is O(n). The sorted list is mutated in place; auxiliary space depends on Python's sort implementation, which may use temporary storage.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum removals needed to make intervals pairwise non-overlapping.
Idea: Sort by start time and greedily retain the interval with the earlier end whenever two overlap.
Technique and why it applies: prev indexes the current interval in the retained set. If the next interval starts before its end, one interval must be removed; replacing prev only when the new interval ends sooner preserves more future options.
Invariant: The retained candidate ending at intervals[prev][1] is the shortest-ending choice among the overlap conflict processed so far.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero because the loop is skipped and prev is never dereferenced. Intervals touching at an endpoint are considered non-overlapping.
Complexity: Sorting and scanning take O(n log n) time. The code uses O(1) explicit auxiliary variables, but Python's in-place sort may use O(n) temporary memory.

Task and constraints: Minimize interval removals so no remaining intervals overlap.
Idea: Sort intervals by ending time and greedily keep each interval that starts at or after the end of the last kept interval.
Technique and why it applies: Earliest-finish-time selection leaves the most room for subsequent intervals. Any interval beginning before right is removed; otherwise it becomes the new retained interval.
Invariant: right is the end of the last kept interval, whose selection maximizes the number of compatible intervals in the processed prefix.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero. Intervals that meet exactly at right are accepted because the overlap test is strict.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(n log n), followed by an O(n) scan. Explicit auxiliary space is O(1), though the in-place sort can allocate temporary memory.

Task and constraints: Return start indices of all substrings of s that are anagrams of p.
Idea: Compare fixed-size character-frequency maps for p and each sliding window in s.
Technique and why it applies: d2 stores p's counts; d1 begins with the first window and is updated by adding the entering character and subtracting the leaving one. Equal maps mean the window is an anagram.
Invariant: Before each comparison, d1 represents exactly the frequency counts of the current window of length len(p).
Edge cases: If p is longer than s, the method returns an empty list. It assumes lowercase English letters because the maps initialize only a-z; other characters would raise KeyError.
Complexity: There are O(n) windows, but each dictionary equality compares 26 entries, a fixed alphabet size. Time is O(n) and the two maps use O(1) space for lowercase letters, plus O(n) output.

Task and constraints: Find all starting positions where a substring of s is a rearrangement of p.
Idea: Use a sliding window and a 26-element balance array that begins with the required counts from p.
Technique and why it applies: Adding a character from s decrements its balance; if that balance becomes negative, the left edge advances and restores counts until the window is valid. A window whose length equals len(p) is an anagram.
Invariant: The balance array reflects the difference between needed p characters and the current window, with the shrinking loop removing excess occurrences.
Edge cases: If p is longer than s, the loop never reaches a window of the needed length and returns empty. The code assumes lowercase English letters.
Complexity: Each index advances monotonically, giving O(n+|p|) time and O(1) auxiliary space for the fixed alphabet. The author labels are correct when n represents combined input length.

Task and constraints: Find the kth integer in lexicographical order among integers from 1 through n.
Idea: Count how many numbers lie under a decimal prefix, then move to a child prefix or the next sibling depending on k.
Technique and why it applies: prefix recursively sums the counts for decimal children when the prefix is within n; the main loop uses that count to skip entire lexicographic subtrees or descend by appending zero.
Invariant: ans is the current prefix and k is the rank remaining relative to that prefix's subtree.
Edge cases: The implementation uses string digit comparisons and special formulas for prefix bounds, so boundary prefixes near n deserve tests. It assumes 1 <= k <= n.
Complexity: Prefix counting can recursively visit many descendants and repeatedly recompute subtree sizes; worst-case behavior is far above the standard O(log n) per step, with recursion and string allocations. Auxiliary space depends on recursion depth and temporary strings.

Task and constraints: Find the largest complete staircase row count that can be built from n coins.
Idea: Test row counts in increasing order and stop at the first triangular number greater than n.
Technique and why it applies: A staircase with i rows uses i(i+1)/2 coins. When that total exceeds n, the preceding row count is the largest feasible answer; exact equality returns immediately.
Invariant: Every row count below the current i has been checked and is feasible unless the method has already returned.
Edge cases: n=0 is not explicitly handled in the loop's exact-match branch but will break at i=1 and return zero. The upper loop limit is extremely large but only a square-root number of iterations are needed before termination.
Complexity: The loop runs O(sqrt(n)) iterations, each with constant work, and uses O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return every value that appears twice in an array of length n whose values lie in [1,n].
Idea: Count occurrences in a dictionary, then collect keys with counts greater than one.
Technique and why it applies: The first pass builds a frequency map. The second pass emits each key whose count exceeds one; under the problem guarantee each value occurs at most twice.
Invariant: hm contains the exact frequency of every value seen in nums after the first loop.
Edge cases: The method does not modify nums. Each duplicated value is emitted once because dictionary keys are unique.
Complexity: Two passes take O(n) expected time and the frequency dictionary uses O(n) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Find values occurring twice in nums, where values are within 1..n and appear once or twice.
Idea: Cyclically place each value at the index equal to value minus one, then report values not in their target positions.
Technique and why it applies: If nums[i] differs from nums[nums[i]-1], swap them into their canonical position. Once no more swaps are possible, a duplicated value cannot occupy its unique target slot for both copies.
Invariant: The placement loop keeps swapping until each current value matches its target or a duplicate blocks further placement.
Edge cases: The algorithm mutates nums. The given value-range and occurrence constraints are necessary for indexing and termination.
Complexity: Each successful swap places at least one value correctly, so the placement pass is O(n) amortized and the reporting pass O(n), with O(1) auxiliary space apart from the output. The author labels are consistent.

Task and constraints: Return all values that appear twice in an array whose values are bounded by the array length.
Idea: Use Counter to compute frequencies and select entries with count exactly two.
Technique and why it applies: Counter maps each distinct value to its occurrence count, and the list comprehension emits only keys with count equal to two.
Invariant: The returned values are exactly the keys in the frequency map satisfying count == 2.
Edge cases: The problem guarantees no value appears more than twice, so count greater than two is not expected. The imported Counter is used directly.
Complexity: Building the counter is O(n) expected time and O(u) auxiliary space for u distinct values, with output space proportional to the number of duplicates.

Task and constraints: Find the values that occur twice, using the array itself as the visitation structure.
Idea: Negate the value at index abs(i)-1 when a value is first encountered; a negative target slot signals a repeat.
Technique and why it applies: Because values lie in 1..n, each value maps to a valid index. The sign records whether that value has been seen before without a separate set or map.
Invariant: After processing each element, the sign at its target index marks whether the corresponding value has appeared.
Edge cases: The method mutates nums by negating entries, and abs is needed because earlier visits may have made current values negative. The input constraints are essential.
Complexity: Each element is processed once, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space excluding the result list. The author labels are correct.

Task and constraints: Count arithmetic subsequences of length at least three, where equal differences hold between consecutive selected values.
Idea: Use a map per ending index that counts subsequences by their final difference.
Technique and why it applies: For each pair j<i, the difference nums[i]-nums[j] forms a length-two sequence and extends every arithmetic subsequence already ending at j with the same difference. Only extensions of length at least three contribute to ans.
Invariant: dp[i][d] counts arithmetic subsequences of length at least two ending at i with difference d.
Edge cases: The snippet uses defaultdict without importing it, so it raises NameError unless that name is provided externally. Negative and large differences are valid dictionary keys.
Complexity: The pair loops take O(n²) expected time and the maps can store O(n²) index-difference entries, so space is O(n²).

Task and constraints: Return the number of arithmetic subsequences of length at least three in A.
Idea: Dynamic-program over pairs, storing counts of subsequences ending at each index grouped by difference.
Technique and why it applies: Every pair i,j creates a length-two sequence for difference A[i]-A[j]. If dp[j] already has that difference, those sequences extend to i and are added to the answer; dp[i] records both pairs and extensions.
Invariant: dp[i][diff] counts arithmetic subsequences of length at least two ending at i with the given difference.
Edge cases: Arrays shorter than three produce zero because no earlier dp[j] can contribute an extension of length three. Counter values are stored in default dictionaries.
Complexity: The nested pair loops take O(n²) expected time and the DP maps use O(n²) space. The code imports collections and is executable as shown.

Task and constraints: Count ordered boomerang triples (i,j,k) where j and k are distinct points at equal distance from pivot i.
Idea: For each pivot, group other points by a computed distance and count ordered pairs sharing a distance.
Technique and why it applies: Each new point at a distance already seen forms a pair with every previous point at that distance; multiplying the prior count by two accounts for both orders of the two endpoints. The helper squares the squared Euclidean distance, which preserves equality of distances.
Invariant: count[d] records how many earlier points have the same distance key from the current pivot.
Edge cases: The code references defaultdict without importing it, so it fails unless that name is available externally. The problem guarantees distinct points, and the pivot itself contributes distance zero only once.
Complexity: For each of n pivots, all n points are scanned, giving O(n²) expected time and O(n) temporary map space. The missing import is a runtime issue.
